title: Sparkling Water 12-pack

drivers.name: Promotion: 20% off
drivers.evidence: Past 20% off promotions had noise-adjusted median lift of x1.58; recent 25% off lifted to x1.55, suggesting 20% may yield ~x1.45–1.55. This week is not a holiday, so lift may be closer to 45%.

drivers.name: Competitor store opening across the street
drivers.evidence: No past data on competitor openings, but new competition introduces demand risk. The product is price-sensitive and in a competitive category. The effect is uncertain but plausible based on market dynamics. Shrink to -15% to reflect low confidence.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 95.5. A 20% discount (19.9% price drop) aligns with past promotions, which had a noise-adjusted lift of x1.58. However, the recent 25% off week (2026-07-20) only lifted sales to x1.55, and the 25% off in a holiday week (2026-06-29) saw a higher x3.5, suggesting context matters. The competitor opening across the street introduces demand risk—this is a new, untested shock. The week after a promotion typically sees a 24% drop (noise-adjusted x0.76), but this is not the post-promo week. Halloween (week before) suppressed sales by x0.68, but this is not the same week. The classical model’s x1.07 is too low. We adjust upward for promotion, but shrink due to thin evidence and new competitive threat. Final median adjusted to x1.45.

  events: Promotion: 20% off
  shelf price: 4.94 (-19.9% vs regular price 6.17)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 95.5 | 5%-95%: 28.9 - 183.3 | 10%-90%: 61.2 - 151.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-39% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
